howBattery_1: The battery is a short-term reserve for hard running. Running faster than about 15 km/h uses it up, and the faster the run, the quicker it goes. Below that pace it refills, fastest at a walk. The more hard running there has been in the match, the slower it refills, so the same rest brings back less late in a game.
howBattery_2: The battery is the D′ balance model from sports science [1, 2, 3]. Critical speed is the fastest pace a runner can keep up for a long time, and D′ is the distance they can run above it before the reserve is gone. For a typical professional we use a critical speed of 4.1 m/s, about 15 km/h [3, 4], and a D′ of 180 m [5]. No study has measured D′ in professional players, so that value comes from university players.
howBattery_3: Critical speed can't be read from tracking data. Studies that tried got about 7 km/h with one method and about 14 km/h with another, and the first study's authors say their value is likely well below the players' true critical speed [6, 7]. So we take both values from fitness tests.
howBattery_4: We can't measure how tired or how fit a player actually is, so the battery shows how much reserve a typical professional would have left after the same running. We run it for 200 typical professionals whose critical speed and D′ are spread around those values [3, 4, 5] and show the middle value.
howBattery_5: The standard model refills too fast for runners, so ours refills four times slower, close to what was measured in runners [8]. Repeated hard efforts slow the refill further, as measured in cyclists [9].
howBattery_6: We added four things to the published model. The research applies it to one athlete whose fitness has been tested; we apply it to every player in a match, from their positions alone. Since we can't test the players, we run it for 200 typical professionals and show the middle one. We made the refill slow down as the match's hard running builds up, with a formula and settings we fitted on simulated matches. And we test the battery on simulated matches where each player's true state is known, which real matches can't offer.

howAgentsTitle: The commentary: written by AI, checked before it is shown
howAgents_1: Our code does the measuring and four AI agents write the words. Every number they get comes with its unit and the measurement it came from.
howAgentStep_1: Tracking of every player and the ball
howAgentStep_2: Our code measures the running and the battery
howAgentStep_5: Agent 2 writes each line from our list of research findings
howAgentStep_6: Agent 3 adapts it for fans or analysts
howAgentStep_7: Agent 4 checks it and blocks what the numbers don't support
howAgents_2: The check has two stages. Fixed rules come first and give the same answer every time: each number has to match the measurement, and a general statement about football has to agree with our list of findings, which we took from sports research by hand. The check does not read the research itself. A second AI then reads the sentence and can block it but can't rewrite it.
howAgents_3: The second AI can give different answers on different runs. The fixed rules always give the same one.
howAgentsCite: The comparisons in the lines and clips, such as a player's top speed against the usual top speed for his position, come from published match studies [10–19].
howDataTitle: What it needs from a real match
howData_1: Tracking data: the position of every player and the ball, 10 times a second, from cameras in the stadium or from the broadcast.
howData_3: Whether the ball is in play and who has it, and match events (passes, turnovers, shots) for some of the moments.
howData_4: Nothing worn by the players: no sensors, GPS vests or fitness tests.
howDataSynthetic: The matches on this site come from our own simulator, built on published sports science, and its sprints follow a published motion model [20]. Because we generate them, we know each player's true state and can test the battery against it. We checked how the simulated players move against tracking data from real professional matches [21] and against Premier League match data [22, 23].
howLiveIntro: We built a live version and ran both matches on this site through it, one frame at a time, the way a stadium feed sends them. It never looks ahead.
howMore: Formulas, tests and the research behind each number:
howBatteryTech: Across the 200 typical professionals, critical speed is 4.1 ± 0.3 m/s and the reserve (D′) 180 ± 54 m. We tuned how much the match's hard running slows the refill on 60 simulated matches and checked it on 110 others. Analysts also see the range that holds the middle 80% of the 200 typical professionals.
howAgentsTech: Built with Microsoft Foundry and Agent Framework (gpt-5-mini). The agents read the measurements through an MCP server.
howLive_1: The live battery came out almost the same as the one on this page: less than half a point apart on average.
howLive_2: Speeds arrive half a second late, because live positions can only be smoothed with what has already happened.
howLive_3: Each second of play takes about 1.5 milliseconds to process, so it easily keeps up with a match: a whole match took under 10 seconds.
howLive_4: Of the 134 times a player reached his hardest minutes in the story match, the live version caught 128, within 30 seconds.
howLive_5: Writing and checking the commentary took about 25 seconds per moment, so lines would follow their moment by about half a minute.

howProfileTitle: {name}: fastest average speed over each length of time
howProfileSub: His whole match. Dashed: 14.8 km/h, the critical speed of a typical pro. Players don't keep up a fast pace for long in a match, so his best averages over 5 or 10 minutes sit far below that line. A critical speed fitted to a curve like this comes out far too low, which is why we take it from fitness tests.
howCompareTitle: {name}'s whole match: the published model and ours
howCompareSub: The same running and the same typical pro (critical speed 4.1 m/s, D′ 180 m). The standard model refills fastest [1]. Ours refills four times slower [8], and slower again as the match's hard running builds up.
howCompareHint: Point at the chart to read the three values.
